card.hook: Picture a chair so big that one of its legs has been snapped off halfway, parked in front of a building full of diplomats. You can read it from across a busy square, and that's what makes it such a good photo.
card.stand_here: Stand at the edge of the Place des Nations, facing the main gate of the Palace of Nations, with the chair in front of the gate. From the square, the chair is to the north-east, so you can also walk up to it for a close-up.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the chair and the palace gates sit together and look natural. If you're far back, try 2x to crop in on the chair and the gate. Use 0.5x only when you're close, and keep the chair away from the corners so it doesn't stretch.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the chair, then slide to darker if the bright sky is washing out the wood.
card.best_time: Early morning is best, when fewer people wander through your shot. The fountain jets can add a foreground, but only in warmer months and only if they're switched on, so don't count on them.
card.selfie_here: Stand right beside the broken leg, at the base of the chair, so it fills the background behind you. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a little low so the chair towers over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand well back on the open paved square, far enough to fit the whole chair in the frame, and shoot toward it from the front while you stand at its base.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed for personal use, but flash may be restricted in some areas of the Place des Nations. Light traffic and trams run through the square, so watch for vehicles when you cross the road for a photo.
card.challenge: Walk up close, aim steeply upwards at the shortened leg, and see if you can make the chair look as huge as it really is.
card.good_to_know: The chair is 12 metres high and uses 5.5 tonnes of wood. Handicap International first put it up in August 1997, meant for three months, and it symbolises opposition to land mines and cluster bombs. Strong public support kept it there until 2005, when the square was remodelled, and it came back to the same place in February 2007.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the edge of the Place des Nations, facing the main gate of the Palace of Nations, with the chair in front of the gate. From the square, the chair is to the north-east, so you can also walk up to it for a close-up.

selfie_spots.why: Standing close puts the chair directly behind you, and the sculpture's size comes across most clearly at close range.

card.hook: Get close to the Jet d'Eau and it stops looking like a fountain and starts looking like a white skyscraper made of water. Nothing else is competing with it, so even a quick snap looks great.
card.stand_here: Walk out along the stone jetty from the left bank to the Jetée du Jet-d'eau and stand at the phone icon, about 20 m north-east of the fountain. Face south-west and the jet is right in front of you, with the lake behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the whole tall column fits, and hold your phone upright. Try 1x for the spray at the base or the top, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the plume against the sky.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white column, then slide to a little darker so the bright water keeps its detail, and switch on gridlines to put the jet on one vertical line.
card.best_time: Come in the evening from spring to autumn, when 21 lights glow on the jet. Use night mode and hold your phone steady against the rail or your body. By day, check the wind first, because a change in direction can soak the jetty.
card.selfie_here: Walk out along the Jetée des Eaux-Vives (the stone jetty) toward its small white lighthouse, where the fountain is closest. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the jet tower over your shoulder. On sunny days the spray can even throw in a rainbow.
card.ask_someone: For a shot with the whole jet rising over the water, stand on the Bains des Pâquis jetty on the right bank, directly across the harbour from the fountain, and hand your phone to a passer-by.
card.rules_and_safety: The fountain can be switched off in frost or strong wind, so check the weather and the official site before you go. Keep a dry cloth handy, because mist covers your phone lens fast.
card.challenge: Catch the spray mid-fall with a Live Photo, then pick the frame where it looks like the jet is wearing a lacy white skirt.
card.good_to_know: The jet shoots about 500 litres of water every second up to 150 metres, leaving the nozzle at around 200 km/h. The first one, in 1886, reached only about 30 metres. It has stood at this spot since 1891, and the present fountain dates from 1951.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk out along the stone jetty from the left bank to the Jetée du Jet-d'eau and stand at the phone icon, about 20 m north-east of the fountain. Face south-west and the jet is right in front of you, with the lake behind it.

selfie_spots.why: Standing on the jetty puts the fountain close and towering behind you, and the spray can catch rainbows on sunny days.

card.hook: Picture a clock you can't wind, made of about 6,500 flowers, with a second hand longer than a car. That's Geneva's Flower Clock, ticking away in the lawn beside the lake.
card.stand_here: Stand on the garden paths at the west end of the Jardin Anglais, by the Quai du Général-Guisan, and face the clock. Use the trees as a frame on one side and keep the clock low in the picture with the lake above it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the dial with the lake behind it. Stay on the paths and 2x pulls the clock in without you walking into the crowd. Go right up to the dial and 0.5x fits the whole face and the sky into one frame.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the dial, then nudge the picture a touch darker if the sky is bright, so the flower colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Summer afternoons bring tour groups around the dial, so be patient and wait for a gap. The planting changes with the seasons and winter displays are usually less colourful, so you'll get a different picture each visit.
card.selfie_here: Try the west side of the Jardin Anglais beside the Quai du Général-Guisan, on the lawn beside the clock face. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the clock over your shoulder, and keep your arm low so the flowers fit in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in front of the Hotel Metropole, which faces the clock, while you stand by the dial, and they can get the whole clock in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Please don't climb onto the clock, as that can damage the flowers and plants. Check the official Geneva city site before you go for any changes.
card.challenge: Crouch low so the flowers fill the bottom of the frame, then wait for the second hand to sweep into the shot.
card.good_to_know: The Flower Clock (L'horloge fleurie) was created in 1955 as a nod to Geneva's watchmakers and to nature. The dial is about 5 metres across. The second hand is 2.5 metres long, said to be the longest in the world.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the garden paths at the west end of the Jardin Anglais, by the Quai du Général-Guisan, and face the clock. Use the trees as a frame on one side and keep the clock low in the picture with the lake above it.

selfie_spots.why: This is where the clock sits, on the left bank beside the lake quay, so it is the spot where the clock is most clearly the backdrop.

card.hook: There's a giant Broken Chair parked in front of the Palace of Nations, and honestly, it's the easiest way to make your photo look like you were really there. Behind it, a row of member-state flags does the rest.
card.stand_here: Walk north towards the flags and the Broken Chair, then stand in Place des Nations on the south side of the Palace's approach. Face the main entrance, which is straight ahead.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the flags, the façade and the chair all in one shot. Switch to 0.5x if you want to get close to the chair and make it look huge. Zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) gives you a tighter shot of the entrance between the flags.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the façade up with the horizontal lines so the long building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Midday or the afternoon is the suggestion, when the sun is high enough to light up the façade. Wait for a few people to walk past the chair, because they show how big it is.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the Broken Chair on Place des Nations, across the square from the Palais entrance. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the chair in the frame. For a colourful backdrop, try a close selfie in front of the row of flags along the approach (the Alley of Flags). No guide describes a selfie with the whole building directly behind you, so check the shot on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the chair's end of Place des Nations and shoot towards you, so the Palais entrance sits beyond you (the wall and trees may hide part of the building, so check the shot).
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine for personal use, but flash is generally prohibited. The Palace is a working diplomatic site, so stay on the public side of the barriers and follow any photography signs.
card.challenge: Get the main entrance sitting neatly between two flags, with the Broken Chair low in the frame in front.
card.good_to_know: The Palace of Nations began as the headquarters of the League of Nations and is now the Geneva home of the United Nations. It was built between 1929 and 1938 by five architects who combined their ideas after a competition with 377 entries. When it was completed in 1936, it was the second-largest building complex in Europe by volume, behind only Versailles.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk north towards the flags and the Broken Chair, then stand in Place des Nations on the south side of the Palace's approach. Face the main entrance, which is straight ahead.

card.hook: Four stone giants, each 5 metres tall, look out over a pond in the middle of a park, and the whole 100-metre wall fits in one photo. That's rare for a monument this big.
card.stand_here: Head into Parc des Bastions: the wall is to the north-east, about 2 minutes on foot. Stand on the broad paved forecourt directly in front of it, with the pond between you and the statues, and face the wall.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole wall in. Go to 0.5x if you want more trees and pond, then 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the four central statues and their carved faces.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the top of the wall up with a horizontal line, then leave a strip of trees at the top and the pond at the bottom.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is best, when the side light is kind to the statues. Late-morning sun hits the faces harder. The wall is also lit at night, so you can go after dark and use night mode with your elbows resting on something firm.
card.selfie_here: Stand directly in front of the centre of the wall, below the four big figures, and use the front camera. Try 0.5x with the statues and the motto stone over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the grass or path opposite the wall, with the big university building behind them, and to step back far enough to fit all 100 metres while you pose in front of the central statues.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are encouraged, but please don't climb on the statues, and keep the noise down. The park is described as safe and well-patrolled, but keep your valuables secure.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole wall, then walk to either end and see if you can catch a completely different view of it.
card.good_to_know: The wall opened in 1909 to mark 400 years since John Calvin's birth and 350 years since the University of Geneva was founded. The four big statues are Farel, Calvin, Beza and Knox. Look for the Latin motto Post Tenebras Lux (After darkness, light) carved along the wall.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head into Parc des Bastions: the wall is to the north-east, about 2 minutes on foot. Stand on the broad paved forecourt directly in front of it, with the pond between you and the statues, and face the wall.

selfie_spots.why: The central statues and the motto-bearing stone give the wall its most recognisable backdrop, which is why guides single it out as the spot to pose against.

The selfie-spot evidence is thin: no page gives an exact camera position, so the central-statue spot is inferred from pages calling the wall a striking backdrop. card.hook: Picture a clock face made entirely of flowers, tilted on a slope so you can read it from the pavement. That's the Horloge Fleurie, and it's the star of the Jardin Anglais.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement in front of the flower clock, a little to one side of the crowds, on the Quai du Général-Guisan side. Face the clock so the flower face is in front of you, with the quay and the garden behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the clock with the quay behind it. Try zoom 0.5x if you want more trees and sky, and keep the clock away from the edges so it doesn't stretch. For a tight shot of the clock face that leaves out passing traffic, go to zoom 2x or higher.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the clock face on the lower third, with the quay and the garden filling the space above it.
card.best_time: Go early morning or late afternoon. It's calmer, the light is softer, and the tour groups haven't arrived yet. The flowers look best in daylight.
card.selfie_here: Try the Monument national by the garden entrance, where the bronze figures stand on their stone pedestal above a round flowerbed. Use the front camera, switch to zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the monument sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the pavement in front of the clock, standing a little to one side to keep the tour groups out of the frame, and pose with the clock behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The clock stands beside a busy road, so keep an eye on the traffic while you line up your shot.
card.challenge: Take a few frames and try to catch the clock face with no car or tour group in sight. It's harder than it sounds.
card.good_to_know: The Jardin Anglais was laid out in 1855 on the site of an old harbour and a wood. It took its present shape in 1863, when the Pont du Mont-Blanc was built. The park also hosts Geneva's annual Christmas Market.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement in front of the flower clock, a little to one side of the crowds, on the Quai du Général-Guisan side. Face the clock so the flower face is in front of you, with the quay and the garden behind it.

card.hook: Geneva's cathedral has a medieval body and a Neo-Classical face, like a knight in a smart 18th-century jacket. Look up over the Old Town rooftops and you'll spot the towers and that green spire easily.
card.stand_here: Stand on Rue Etienne-Dumont, near Place du Bourg-de-Four. From the Place du Bourg-de-Four the cathedral is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot, so walk that way and face the cathedral for a close, street-level view.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view from the street. If the street is too narrow to fit the towers in, switch to 0.5x. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details like the spire and towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, keep the phone level so the towers stand straight, then tap the cathedral and drag the brightness slider a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the stonework than harsh midday sun. Late afternoon also suits the courtyard out front.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Cour de Saint-Pierre, the courtyard in front of the cathedral, and stand in front of the neo-classical portico, ideally in late afternoon. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone a bit high so the portico sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo on Rue Etienne-Dumont near Place du Bourg-de-Four, the street spot that gives the best view of the cathedral, and ask them to keep the cathedral in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The cathedral is a working church and the tower climb is paid, so check the official site before you go. The tower stairs are steep and narrow, both going up and coming down. The streets here are for walking, so step aside and let others pass while you shoot.
card.challenge: Find the green spire peeking above the rooftops and get it straight on your gridlines, with no leaning towers allowed.
card.good_to_know: The present building was begun around 1160 in the Gothic style, and the classical portico was added in the 18th century. It has been the principal church of the Protestant Church of Geneva since 1535, and John Calvin preached here. Below the cathedral there's an archaeological site, a reminder of how long people have used this hill.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Rue Etienne-Dumont, near Place du Bourg-de-Four. From the Place du Bourg-de-Four the cathedral is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot, so walk that way and face the cathedral for a close, street-level view.

card.hook: Cafe terraces on this square have a sneaky habit of spreading right up to the fountain, so your first job is to find a clear gap. The cobbles, the tall old houses and the fountain all fit in one frame, which makes this an easy photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place du Bourg-de-Four, right beside the small marble fountain, and face uphill. The fountain sits low in front of you and the tall old houses and cafe terraces rise up behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the fountain-and-houses shot. Switch to 0.5x to take in the lower part of the square with its people and cafes. For the cathedral towers over the northern row of houses, try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the fountain on one of the lower crossing points, and hold your phone level so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Late morning gives you sun without the lunch crowd, and late afternoon is also a good pick. In good weather the terraces fill up and can hide the fountain, so wait a moment or shuffle a step or two.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at the 18th-century fountain at the lower, wider end of the square, with the cafes and houses behind you. Another option is the King Gondebaud statue at the centre of the square. If the fountain is covered or under construction on your visit, the statue is your backup.
card.ask_someone: Stand by the fountain and ask someone near the spot where Rue Etienne-Dumont steps into the square to take your photo.
card.challenge: Turn to the northern row of houses and zoom in until you can see the twin towers of Saint-Pierre Cathedral peeking over the roofs.
card.good_to_know: This square sits on the site of the old Roman forum and a medieval market. In the 19th century it was a stagecoach stop. The marble fountain dates from the 18th century, and the houses around it are from the 16th to 18th centuries.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Place du Bourg-de-Four, right beside the small marble fountain, and face uphill. The fountain sits low in front of you and the tall old houses and cafe terraces rise up behind it.

selfie_spots.name: The 18th-century fountain at the lower, wider end of Place du Bourg-de-Four
selfie_spots.detail: on the café-ringed fountain at the lower end of the square
selfie_spots.why: Guides describe the fountain as the square's visual centrepiece and a ready-made photo subject, so it is the most dependable anchor for a selfie with the square around you.

selfie_spots.detail: at the centre of Place du Bourg-de-Four, by the statue of the Burgundian king
selfie_spots.why: A listing for the square names the statue as a highlight at its centre, which gives a second visible focal point to stand near with the square around you.

selfie_research.notes: Doubtful: no page I found describes a selfie position with the whole square directly behind the visitor, so both selfie spots are inferred from fountain and statue descriptions rather than a stated selfie tip. The airial listing is an aggregator page, so treat the statue spot as weaker. The Rue Etienne Dumont viewpoint is described as a panorama of the cathedral, not of the square, so it is only a rough passer-by option; the pages give no spot that frames the whole square. One Wanderlog review reports the fountain was under construction during one visit, so check on the day. No page gives selfie stick or tripod rules, and no page gives a safety point for this square.

card.hook: A duke left his whole fortune to Geneva with one condition: build me a very grand tomb. The city did, and it's gloriously over the top, with white marble spires, stone lions and a duke lying under his own canopy.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Jardin des Alpes, across the park from the monument, facing it with the lake and the Jet d'Eau behind it. Step back across the lawns until the spire and the fountain sit together in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the classic view with the fountain behind. Go 0.5x to fit the whole platform and the lawns, or 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out the spire and statues and pull the Jet d'Eau closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white marble, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the stone keeps its detail instead of turning flat white.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and kinder to the marble. One guide also suggests sunset.
card.selfie_here: Try the park paths and benches around the monument in the Jardin des Alpes, or the Cottage Café terrace, which overlooks the monument, the Jet d'Eau and Mont-Blanc. Use the front camera, go to 0.5x, and tuck the monument in behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the park in the Jardin des Alpes, facing the monument, while you stand in front of it, so the whole structure and the distant Jet d'Eau fit in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: The inside is generally closed, but you can walk around the outside and take photos from there. Check for seasonal works along the lakeside paths before you go.
card.challenge: Get the spire on one gridline and the Jet d'Eau in the same frame, then see if you can spot a lion and a chimera guarding the platform.
card.good_to_know: The monument was built for Charles II, Duke of Brunswick, who asked for a grand tomb modelled on the Scaliger Tombs in Verona. It was unveiled on 14 October 1879, and the platform is 65 metres long and 25 metres wide. Part of his legacy also paid for the Grand Théâtre.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Jardin des Alpes, across the park from the monument, facing it with the lake and the Jet d'Eau behind it. Step back across the lawns until the spire and the fountain sit together in one frame.

selfie_spots.name: Terrace of the Cottage Café, by the Brunswick Monument
selfie_spots.detail: on the Cottage Café terrace, which overlooks the monument, the Jet d'Eau and Mont-Blanc
selfie_spots.why: A page photographed the monument, the fountain and the mountain from this terrace, so it is a named vantage point close to the monument.

sources.title: Monument Brunswick, Genève - Das Genève

selfie_spots.name: Jardin des Alpes pathways and benches near the monument
selfie_spots.detail: on the park paths and benches around the monument in the Jardin des Alpes
selfie_spots.why: A guide says the park's benches and pathways allow varied compositions, so a visitor could pose with the monument behind on these paths.

sources.title: Brunswick Monument (2026) - Airial

ask_someone_spot.name: Across the park in the Jardin des Alpes, facing the monument
ask_someone_spot.detail: stand across the park from the monument so the whole structure fits in the frame, with the Jet d'Eau in the distance

sources.title: Brunswick Monument (2026) - Airial

rules.rule: The monument's interior is generally closed to visitors, but people may walk around the outside and take photos from there.

sources.title: Brunswick Monument Geneva: Free Audio Guide & Tours - Access Travel

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where the monument sits directly behind a visitor's selfie; the spots above are named viewpoints and I could not confirm them as selfie positions. The Cottage Café's exact location is not given, only that its terrace has a view of the monument. The Jardin des Alpes spot is a general suggestion about pathways and benches, not a named point. The ask-someone spot is a page's advice on framing the monument, not a spot for photographing a person. No page mentions selfie stick or tripod rules, and no page gives a safety point specific to this site.

card.hook: Picture a glass-and-iron dome rising out of a ring of palms, with a big open lawn laid out in front like a red carpet. That's the glasshouse everyone photographs here, and it earns it.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the domed temperate glasshouse, on the exterior view across the lawn. Face west, because the dome lies that way, across the grass.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole glasshouse and the lawn in front of it. Go 0.5x for more sky and foreground, but keep the dome in the middle so the edges don't stretch. Zoom 2x to 5x is great for the dome and the palms close to the glass.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the glasshouse, then slide the brightness down a little so the bright glass and sky keep their detail.
card.best_time: Softer morning or late-afternoon light suits the glass and the plants. Overcast days are good too, because there's less glare on the glass.
card.selfie_here: Stand outside on the path or lawn in front of the domed temperate glasshouse with the dome behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the dome over your shoulder. The pond with swans in the outdoor gardens is a nice spot to pause for photos too.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site before you go for opening times, any closures, and whether the glasshouse gallery needs a separate ticket.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the dome just off-centre with the lawn filling the bottom third, and keep the glasshouse walls dead straight. Bonus points if no palm tree is sprouting out of anyone's head.
card.good_to_know: The garden was founded in 1817 by Augustin Pyramus de Candolle and now covers 28 hectares. About 700,000 visits were recorded in 2023, which made it the city's most visited attraction. The whole garden, including the greenhouses and the two mansions, is registered as a cultural asset of national importance.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the domed temperate glasshouse, on the exterior view across the lawn. Face west, because the dome lies that way, across the grass.

selfie_spots.name: Domed temperate glasshouse, Jardin Botanique de Genève
selfie_spots.detail: outside on the path or lawn in front of the domed temperate glasshouse, with the dome behind you
selfie_spots.why: A guide photo shows the dome under a blue sky with trees around it, which makes it the most distinctive landmark backdrop found.

sources.title: Geneva Botanical Garden: Free Entry, Hours and Glasshouses

selfie_spots.name: Pond with swans, Jardin Botanique de Genève
selfie_spots.detail: beside the pond in the outdoor gardens, where swans glide
selfie_spots.why: A Geneva engagement photographer names this pond as a place to pause for photos, though no page says it works as a backdrop showing the garden.

sources.title: Switzerland Engagement Photographer – Romantic Geneva Session

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a passer-by photo position that shows the whole garden, so ask_someone_spot is null. The selfie spots are less specific than requested: the glasshouse entry comes from a tourism page's photo captions and the pond entry is from a photographer's session blog that does not describe a selfie backdrop. The 'flower clock' pages refer to the Jardin Anglais, a different park, so I excluded them. No page stated selfie stick or tripod rules, and no safety point was mentioned.

card.hook: Geneva's busiest bridge is also its best photo prop: the lake spreads out on one side, and on the other the Rhône starts flowing away. Stand back on the quay and watch the whole city funnel across it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Quai du Mont-Blanc, the lakeside promenade right next to the bridge. It's about 2 minutes on foot from the middle of the bridge, and the bridge lies to the south-east, so face that way and look across at it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the bridge, the quay and the lake in one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer view of the bridge with the city behind it. If your phone has 2x to 5x, use it to pick out the Jet d'Eau or the mountains in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the bridge along a lower third with water in front, and keep the horizon level, because a long bridge shows every tilt.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light on the mountains is best. Mont Blanc only shows on clear days, so count it as a bonus.
card.selfie_here: Walk onto the bridge's western walkway, where the flags line the footway, and use the front camera at 0.5x with the flags over your shoulder. One guide also says the western side has the best sunset views. For a different mood, take the stairs down to the lake-level path under the north side of the bridge for sweeping views across La Rade towards the Jet d'Eau.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by near either end of the bridge, on the city-centre side as you walk toward the Flower Clock, to photograph you with the bridge in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Traffic is heavy and it gets busy at peak times. Cyclists are sometimes pushed onto the pavement, so keep clear of them when you set up.
card.challenge: Take a quick burst and catch the one moment when the bridge looks calm, with a gap in the traffic and nobody in your way.
card.good_to_know: The Pont du Mont-Blanc was inaugurated in 1862 and is about 250 metres long. It's named after Mont Blanc, the highest massif in the Alps, which you can see from the city on a clear day. It also marks the point where Lake Geneva's harbour, the Rade de Genève, turns into the Rhône. A few metres to the west, in the river, sits the little Ile Rousseau.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Quai du Mont-Blanc, the lakeside promenade right next to the bridge. It's about 2 minutes on foot from the middle of the bridge, and the bridge lies to the south-east, so face that way and look across at it.

selfie_spots.name: Pedestrian walkway under the north side of Pont du Mont-Blanc
selfie_spots.detail: Reached by a set of stairs from Quai du Mont-Blanc or Quai des Bergues, on the lake-level path under the bridge
selfie_spots.why: This view brings you close to the waters of Lac Leman as well as sweeping views across La Rade towards the Jet d'Eau.

sources.title: Pont du Mont-Blanc, Switzerland (Locationscout)

selfie_spots.name: The bridge's own pedestrian walkway, on the western side
selfie_spots.detail: On the bridge deck itself, where the flags line the footway
selfie_spots.why: It is a great photo spot thanks to the flags on both sides. A guide also says the western side of the bridge offers the best sunset views.

Pont du Mont-Blanc Geneva (2025) (Airial)

ask_someone_spot.detail: The approach on foot from the city centre; a reviewer recommends walking toward the Flower Clock to photograph the bridge

sources.title: Geneva - Switzerland - Mont Blanc Bridge - Good for the Views (Tripadvisor)

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot with the bridge directly behind a selfie-taker on the ground; the selfie spots above are the closest supported options, and the first is a lake-level viewpoint with the bridge overhead rather than behind. The ask-someone spot is a general vantage suggestion, not a named point on a map, so verify it before use. The Dailysabah Flower Clock corner (where the road to the bridge meets Quai du Général-Guisan) is named as a photo spot for the Flower Clock, not the bridge, so I left it out. No page mentioned selfie stick or tripod rules, and no safety point was stated. Crowding and traffic are mentioned, and one source says cyclists are pushed onto the pavement, but I did not use these as safety points.

card.hook: Some museums want you to rush inside. This one is happy for you to stand outside first, with plenty of calm open space around the buildings, and take a nice wide photo.
card.stand_here: Find the phone icon on the map. It sits in the middle of the outline of the International Committee of the Red Cross headquarters, right beside the museum. Walk a little way from there, then turn to face the museum and pick your view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural look at the buildings. Switch to zoom 0.5x if you want to squeeze more of them into one frame. Then try zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for signs, flags and entrances.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the edges of the walls up with them, and keep the phone level so the tall walls don't lean inwards.
card.best_time: Soft daylight works best on big buildings, so go for a bright overcast day, or the morning or late afternoon.
card.selfie_here: One guide says the reflection pool beside the museum, outside Avenue de la Paix 17, mirrors the building. Use the front camera, stand at the pool and let the facade and its reflection sit behind you in the water. No page gives its exact spot on the map, so have a look around when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone on the forecourt in front of the entrance facade (Avenue de la Paix 17) and ask for a wide shot of the whole building with you in it, standing a little way back from the facade so it all fits.
card.rules_and_safety: The museum may have ticketed entry and set hours, so check the official site before you go. If you plan to take photos inside, check there too, because the interior photography rules aren't covered here.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole setting, then one zoom 2x close-up of a flag, sign or entrance, with the walls dead straight in both.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened in 1988 and holds about 30,000 items. One of them is the first Nobel Peace Prize medal, awarded jointly in 1901 to Red Cross founder Henry Dunant and the French pacifist Frédéric Passy. It also holds the archives of the International Prisoners of War Agency, which UNESCO has listed in its Memory of the World Register.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Find the phone icon on the map. It sits in the middle of the outline of the International Committee of the Red Cross headquarters, right beside the museum. Walk a little way from there, then turn to face the museum and pick your view.

selfie_spots.name: Reflection pool outside the museum, Avenue de la Paix 17
selfie_spots.detail: on the pool beside the museum building, with the facade reflected in the water behind you
selfie_spots.why: One guide says the pool's mirror-like surface reflects the museum building, which makes a backdrop for a selfie, though no page places it exactly on a map.

sources.title: International Red Cross Museum Geneva - Access Travel

ask_someone_spot.name: Front facade of the museum, Avenue de la Paix 17
ask_someone_spot.detail: on the forecourt in front of the museum's entrance facade on Avenue de la Paix 17; no page gives a set standing point for the photographer

sources.title: International Red Cross Museum Geneva - Access Travel
Everything You Need to Know About Visiting International Museum of the Red Cross and Red Crescent - US News Travel

selfie_research.notes: Evidence is thin. The only page naming a spot with the museum behind (the reflection pool) is a generic-looking listing with no exact location, so verify on site. The facade is the landmark itself, so the ask-someone spot gives the whole building but not a stand-off position. The outdoor Leutwyler 'Humanity' photo display along the lake (Quai Wilson) is named in one blog and another guide calls it photogenic, but no page puts the museum behind a visitor there, so I left it out. The Red Cross Garden and balcony named by the Access Travel page are not confirmed by other sources. No page mentions selfie sticks or tripods. The only photography rule found (flash not allowed, filming permitted) is not a selfie-stick or tripod rule, so I left it out.

card.hook: Picture a neo-classical stone palace rising straight out of the Rhône, with tall arched windows glowing as the sky goes blue. It looks like it's floating, and it's even better than it sounds.
card.stand_here: Stand on Pont de la Coulouvrenière, roughly 75 m from the Bâtiment des Forces motrices. Face the building so its riverside façade rises out of the water with the bridge framing it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the whole façade and the bridge fit in the shot. Then try 2x to pick out the arched windows and the stonework. Zoom 0.5x gets more of the bridge in, but keep the building away from the edges so it doesn't stretch.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then slide the brightness a touch darker so the lit windows don't blow out.
card.best_time: Go in the evening or at blue hour, when the building is lit up. At night, switch on night mode and hold your phone steady against your body while it takes the shot.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt it slightly upward so the building sits over your shoulder. Check the arched windows are in the frame before you smile.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Pont de la Coulouvrenière to frame the whole building from the bridge while you step into the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your phone away from the railing edge and watch for passing cyclists and pedestrians while you frame the shot. Take extra care on the bridge after dark. The building is usually open only on event nights, so treat the outside as your main photo.
card.challenge: Get the glowing arched windows, a ribbon of river and a bit of bridge into one shot, with the building sitting neatly on a gridline third.
card.good_to_know: The building was put up between 1883 and 1892 as the power house of a hydro plant and waterworks. It used the river's flow to supply water pressure for the city's drinking water and for local workshops, including watchmakers. It stopped working as a power source in 1963 and reopened in 1997 as an opera house and concert hall.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Pont de la Coulouvrenière, roughly 75 m from the Bâtiment des Forces motrices. Face the building so its riverside façade rises out of the water with the bridge framing it.

ask_someone_spot.name: Pont de la Coulouvrenière
ask_someone_spot.detail: Ask the passer-by to stand on the bridge and frame the whole building from there; a guide lists the building as seen from this bridge.

sources.title: Visiting Bâtiment des Forces Motrices Geneva - Tickets, Hours, and Travel Guide (audiala)

selfie_research.safety: A 2013 blog post says the bridge where its author shot the building was very dark and that a group of drunken youths loitered too close, so take care after dark.
selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the building behind the visitor, so selfie_spots is empty rather than guessed. The Pont de la Machine guide mentions a picturesque foreground, but only for lake and Jet d'Eau views, not the building, so I excluded it. The Quai du Seujet is named as a waterfront location where the building sits on the water, and Wikimedia Commons names Quai des Forces-Motrices as a viewpoint, but neither page describes a selfie position; they are alternatives for a passer-by shot. No page mentions selfie stick or tripod rules. Your position is roughly 75 m from the building's listed coordinates. The Pont de la Coulouvrenière source is a travel guide that mentions the building viewed from that bridge, so verify the exact framing on site.

card.hook: Picture a general on a bronze horse trying to upstage an opera house. General Dufour's statue nearly pulls it off, but the grand Second Empire facade behind him wins, with its eight big limestone pillars and six smaller red granite ones.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place de Neuve, across the square from the main facade. The theatre is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot, so walk across the square and face it with General Dufour's statue in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the whole facade and the statue fit in one frame. If you're close and the building won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the pediment, the sculptures and the composer busts under the roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the facade's vertical edges with them so the building doesn't lean, and tap the facade, then slide darker if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Golden hour suits the outside of the building. In the evening the facade is lit up, so switch on night mode and hold your phone steady against your body while it captures.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the square in front of the main facade, on the Place de Neuve 3 side, with the theatre behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x so the whole building fits over your shoulder, and check the spot on the ground.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the Parc des Bastions, opposite the theatre, so the full building fits in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Place de Neuve is a public open-air square, so no ticket is needed outside. The auditorium and grand staircase are indoors and need a performance or tour ticket, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Zoom in and find all four marble statues (Drama, Dance, Music and Comedy), then get one photo with the statue of the general tucked low in the corner.
card.good_to_know: The theatre was inaugurated in 1879 with Rossini's William Tell. A fire in 1951 destroyed the stage and auditorium, but the facades survived. It reopened in 1962 and still has the largest stage in Switzerland.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Place de Neuve, across the square from the main facade. The theatre is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot, so walk across the square and face it with General Dufour's statue in front of you.

selfie_spots.name: Place de Neuve, on the square in front of the theatre facade
selfie_spots.detail: on the square in front of the building's main facade, at the Place de Neuve 3 side
selfie_spots.why: The square is the theatre's front open space, and the facade is the part sources call most photogenic, so it makes a strong backdrop.

sources.title: Geneva Arts Guide: Theatres, Galleries and Festivals
Grand Théâtre — Patrimoine architectural genevois
Grand Théâtre de Genève - Tripadvisor

ask_someone_spot.name: Parc des Bastions, facing the theatre
ask_someone_spot.detail: in the Parc des Bastions, standing opposite the theatre so the full building fits in the frame

sources.title: Grand Théâtre de Genève - Tripadvisor
Geneva Arts Guide: Theatres, Galleries and Festivals

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot was supported. No page I found names a spot where a visitor stands with the theatre behind them, so the Place de Neuve pick is inferred from the square and facade descriptions and should be checked on the ground. The Parc des Bastions position is also inferred from 'opposite the park' wording; no page gives a exact photo point. The interior ceiling and staircase are often named as photo subjects, but they are indoors and not a backdrop for a selfie. Pages say photography is usually restricted during performances and that professional shoots need authorisation; these are venue photo rules, not selfie stick or tripod rules, so they are not listed under rules. The Airial and Geneva Arts Guide sources are general travel pages rather than a dedicated photo guide.

card.hook: Here's a grand stone museum with a digital countdown clock stuck on its face, and it's sneakier to photograph than it looks. The big facade is hard to get right, so treat this one as a patient shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Promenade de l'Observatoire, the small park facing the museum, and face the museum across the park. From Les Tranchées, the museum is to the south-west, about 2 minutes on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole facade, and drop to 0.5x only if trees or railings crowd you. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the sculptures on the gable.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them, so the facade doesn't lean, and leave a little sky above the gable.
card.best_time: Go when the facade is evenly lit, like a bright overcast day or soft evening light. If a projection show happens to be on, a night shot could be a bonus, but we can't promise one.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the building over your shoulder. Step back until the gable fits above your head.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the Promenade de l'Observatoire facing the museum across the park, so the whole facade is in frame, while you stand with the museum behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep flash off inside, as some temporary exhibitions ban photos completely. Check the signs at the entrance for the current rules.
card.challenge: Move a little left or right until the Jet d'Eau pops up between the buildings, then snap it with a 2x to 5x zoom for your second picture.
card.good_to_know: The Musée d'Art et d'Histoire was designed by Marc Camoletti and built between 1903 and 1910 with money left by the banker Charles Galland. It holds more than 650,000 objects, from archaeology to watchmaking. The upper frieze carries the names of Genevan artists, and since 2021 the facade has also carried Gianni Motti's countdown clock.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Promenade de l'Observatoire, the small park facing the museum, and face the museum across the park. From Les Tranchées, the museum is to the south-west, about 2 minutes on foot.

ask_someone_spot.name: Promenade de l'Observatoire (park facing the museum facade)
ask_someone_spot.detail: Stand in the Promenade de l'Observatoire park and face the museum across the park, so the whole facade on Rue Charles-Galland is in frame. The source calls this a challenging facade to shoot, and it is best in the right conditions, such as during a projection mapping show.

sources.title: 10 Places to Photograph in Geneva (Medium, hulobok)

rules.rule: Flash and tripods are prohibited at the Musée d'Art et d'Histoire, and photos are totally banned for some temporary exhibitions.

sources.title: Photographier au musée: Genève entre interdiction et incitation (Tribune de Genève)

rules.rule: Tripods and flash photography are usually not permitted, because they can disrupt other visitors and damage artworks.

sources.title: Musée d'Art et d'Histoire (MAH) (Airial)

rules.rule: Photography for personal, non-commercial use is usually allowed in the permanent collections, but flash should be off, and the posted rules at the entrance should be checked.

sources.title: Geneva History Museum: Unearthing Centuries of Swiss Heritage and Culture (Wonderful Museums)

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the museum behind the visitor, so selfie_spots is empty. The only outdoor photo spot named (Promenade de l'Observatoire) faces the museum, so it works for a passer-by photo instead. The Medium guide is about 6 years old, and the Tribune de Genève rules article is much older, so check current rules at the museum. A Ville de Genève contest page mentions selfies taken inside the museum's rooms, but that is not a landmark-behind spot. No page mentioned selfie sticks, so no stick rule is listed.

card.hook: Two grey lumps of granite sit all alone in Geneva's harbour, and plenty of people stroll right past them. Give them a minute, because the bigger one is the starting point for every height measurement in Switzerland.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Jardin Anglais, on the lakeside edge of the park, and look out over the harbour to the north-east. The two granite boulders sit out in the water with the lake and moored boats behind them.
card.zoom: Start with a wider shot at zoom 1x so the lake and boats set the scene. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a closer picture of the rocks, since they look small from the shore.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the bigger stone on one line and the horizon on the top or bottom line, and leave some empty water around the rocks so they look properly alone.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the granite and the water. Quieter times of day make it easier to grab a clear spot at the water's edge.
card.selfie_here: Try the lakeside promenade on Quai Gustave-Ador, opposite the two stones, and turn your back to the water so they sit behind you. The Jardin Anglais viewpoint over the water works too. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and keep your face off to one side so the stones don't vanish, because they'll look small.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the quay shore at Quai Gustave-Ador facing the water while you stand with the two stones behind you. A short distance back is enough to fit the whole rock group in.
card.rules_and_safety: Swimming isn't allowed in this part of the lake, so enjoy the stones from the shore.
card.challenge: Get one photo with a dead-level horizon, the big stone on a gridline and a moored boat tucked in behind it.
card.good_to_know: The Rhone glacier left these two boulders behind at the end of the last ice age. The larger one, the Repère, was Guillaume-Henri Dufour's height starting point for his 19th-century maps, and it's still the reference for height measurement in Switzerland. The name Niton comes from Neptune, the water god, and the square holes in the top of the big stone, noticed in 1660, may date from the Bronze Age.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Jardin Anglais, on the lakeside edge of the park, and look out over the harbour to the north-east. The two granite boulders sit out in the water with the lake and moored boats behind them.

card.hook: Picture a tiny island of trees sitting in the middle of a river, with a philosopher's statue standing guard. That's Île Rousseau, and it's one of the calmest photo spots in Geneva.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Pont des Bergues, at the footbridge end on the island side. The island is about 1 minute on foot to the north-east, so face north-east and you'll see its tree-lined park, the Rhône flowing past and the Jet d'Eau in view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the island, river and trees together. Switch to 0.5x if you want the bridge gateway big in the foreground, then save a little zoom (2x) for the statue once you've walked across.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the island's trees along one of the lower lines and let the river lead into the shot.
card.best_time: It looks good by day and at night, so pick whichever mood you like. If you're staying nearby, come back at a different hour and get both.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the footbridge where it leaves the Pont des Bergues toward the island, since the bridge is named as a photo spot. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the island and trees fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Pont des Bergues at the end that leads to the island footbridge, while you stand on the footbridge with the island behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a public park reached by a bridge. No closures or restrictions turned up, but check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get a shot where the bridge railing frames the island, then see if you can match it after dark.
card.good_to_know: Île Rousseau is a small island park in the middle of the Rhône in Geneva. It's named after the philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau, and his statue stands on the island. A bridge links the island to the shore, so you can walk across for a close-up of the statue.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Pont des Bergues, at the footbridge end on the island side. The island is about 1 minute on foot to the north-east, so face north-east and you'll see its tree-lined park, the Rhône flowing past and the Jet d'Eau in view.

selfie_spots.why: The island's charming bridge is named as a photo spot, and the footbridge is the approach to the island.

card.hook: Picture a row of plain apartment blocks, then a burst of gold onion domes sitting right in the middle of them. That's the Russian Church, and it's a bit of a showoff.
card.stand_here: Head for the corner of Rue Rodolphe-Toepffer (at Rue François-Le-Fort), on the small rise. The church is to the north of it, about 1 minute on foot, so you can take your first photo before you walk up. Face the church front.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole front of the church in. Then try 2x to pick out the domes and the striped porch, and use 0.5x if you get up close and want it all in the shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the church centred and the walls straight, and tap the golden domes, then drag the slider a touch darker so the gold keeps its detail against a bright sky.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day when the sun is on the front of the church, so the gold looks warm. If the sky is dull, nudge the picture a little brighter to bring out the porch stripes.
card.selfie_here: Switch to the front camera, step back a little and turn so the golden domes sit over your shoulder. Try 0.5x if your phone has it, so more of the church fits in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a working place of worship with limited opening hours, and photography isn't allowed inside. Keep your photos to the outside and check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get three shots: one wide with some street in the foreground, one tight on the domes, and one of the porch stripes.
card.good_to_know: The full name is the Cathedral of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. It was designed by David Grimm of the Imperial Academy of Arts and finished in 1866. It was restored in 1966 and is still a working church today.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the corner of Rue Rodolphe-Toepffer (at Rue François-Le-Fort), on the small rise. The church is to the north of it, about 1 minute on foot, so you can take your first photo before you walk up. Face the church front.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific spot with the Russian Church behind a visitor, or a specific spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole church, so I have left both lists empty rather than guess. The pages describe the church and its gilded domes, and say it stands on a small rise at the corner of Rue Rodolphe-Toepffer and Rue François-Le-Fort, but they do not name a photo position. Sources disagree on the street number (9, 6 or 18 Rue de Beaumont/Rodolphe-Toepffer), so check the address on a map before walking there. Several sources say photography is restricted or prohibited inside the church, and some say it is often restricted during services; I did not list this as a rule because it is not about selfie sticks or tripods. No page I found mentions selfie stick or tripod rules, and no safety point was stated.

card.hook: There's a big old paddle steamer sitting on Lake Geneva that hasn't sailed since 1973, and she still looks like she's about to leave. Paddle boxes, long hull, tall funnel: she's got more character than most things on the waterfront.
card.stand_here: Stand on Embarcadère du Mont-Blanc and turn to face east. The Genève is moored a short way east of the Mont-Blanc landing stage, about 5 minutes on foot, but you can stay on the pier and zoom in.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a scene-setter with the pier, lake and boat. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the hull and paddle boxes, since she's fairly far from the pier. Use 0.5x only if you walk right up to her, and watch for stretched edges.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the boat, then drag the brightness slider down a touch if the sky is bright so the white paintwork keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives soft light on the boat when you face east, because the sun is behind you. Calm, still mornings give the cleanest reflections on the water.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, try 0.5x, and turn so the boat sits over your shoulder. Check she's in the frame before you smile, because she's easy to lose at a distance.
card.rules_and_safety: The pier and lakeside promenade are public places. If you want to visit the boat itself or her summer restaurant, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take two shots: one tight on the funnel and paddle box, one wide with the quay, the water and the boat together. Then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: Genève was built in 1896 and is the oldest paddle ship on Lake Geneva. Her steam engines were swapped for diesel in the 1930s, but she kept the paddle-boat shape. She was taken out of service in 1973, and now she's moored at the Eaux-Vives dock and serves as a restaurant in the summer months.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Embarcadère du Mont-Blanc and turn to face east. The Genève is moored a short way east of the Mont-Blanc landing stage, about 5 minutes on foot, but you can stay on the pier and zoom in.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the paddle steamer Genève itself as the subject. The Geneva pages cover the Jet d'Eau, not this ship, so I left selfie_spots empty rather than substitute a Jet d'Eau viewpoint. Quai du Mont-Blanc, Quai Gustave-Ador and Bains des Pâquis are named only for Jet d'Eau views, so I did not use them. The Wikidata entry for the ship lists coordinates (46°12'17.42"N, 6°9'15.44"E) that match your position, but it does not name a pier or quay, so I could not turn that into a findable spot. No page I found gives selfie-stick or tripod rules for this ship or these quays. A Genevatourism page mentions the Bains des Pâquis pier and Quai Gustave-Ador as photo points for the Jet d'Eau, and a Tourisme Haute-Savoie page notes the Jet d'Eau is visible from the Wilson Quays, but neither ties them to the steamer. A few more targeted searches for the Genève's CGN pier or the Quai du Mont-Blanc sailing point could fill this gap.
